title: Rhythm that bends
summary: Clap a dotted or syncopated rhythm until it is steady, before a single key is pressed.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A bar of four beats: a note held across the first two beats, a short note on the third, and a rest on the fourth. This is an example of the long-short shape a dotted rhythm makes, clapped and counted before a single key is pressed.

steps.title: Rhythm that bends
steps.body:
A dotted rhythm holds a note a little longer and clips the one after it short. Syncopation puts the accent where you do not expect it, on the offbeat instead of the beat. Both feel wrong on the keys until the rhythm is already sure in your body.

1. Find the hard bar's rhythm on the page and clap it alone, counting out loud, with no keys touched.
2. Clap it again, slower, until every long note and every short note lands exactly where it should.
3. Play the bar on one single note, any note, with that same rhythm, ignoring pitch for now.
4. Play the bar with its real notes, slowly first, then back up to tempo.

Clapping first separates two hard jobs into one at a time: the rhythm, then the notes. Trying to learn both at once is how a bent rhythm quietly straightens itself out by accident.

figure.alt: The same long-short-rest bar, clapped first, then played on one note with the real rhythm, before the real notes are added.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: clap the hard bar's rhythm, counting out loud, no keys
Sitting 2: clap it slower until it is steady, then play it on one note
Sitting 3: play the real notes with the rhythm, slowly, five times
Sitting 4: the whole piece at tempo, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, listening for any rhythm that bends

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the name of the piece, then play it once through, hands in the frame.

extras.title: A bar that bends the beat
extras.body:
Compose one bar of your own that plays a trick on the listener's sense of the beat.

Start with a question: what if the beat you expect arrives a little late on purpose?

Three constraints: use one dotted rhythm in the bar, keep it to four beats total, and land squarely on the beat at the end.

Sketch first: write the rhythm as long and short marks on paper before you play a single note.

You know it works when someone else can clap your bar back correctly after hearing it only twice.
